# These are small cars!

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

source("R/book_setup.R")
```

![TwoRed on the day it arrived, on the narrow tires it left the factory with. I'm six feet tall, which gives you the scale. **The silver band running around the car isn't trim — it's the safety cell**, and chapter 2 comes back to it.](images/TwoRed/twored_day_one.jpg){#fig-day-one}

That's the reaction, and it's usually delivered as an exclamation rather than a question.

It's worth being concrete about how small, because the rest of this book doesn't make much sense otherwise. Two seats, and no back seat at all — not a small one, none. **The luggage space behind them is about the size of the boot of an ordinary car with the boot floor raised to the window line.** Before the Dalton Highway I bought a spare wheel to carry, and it barely fitted.

Here's the other measure, and it's the one I can point at today. **TwoRed and Bordeaux both live in our building's parking structure in Honolulu, side by side in a single space marked out for one ordinary car — and between them they don't come close to filling it.**

## It isn't a shrunken car. It's a car built around a box.

Most small cars are ordinary cars made smaller. A Smart isn't. Mercedes started from the steel cell you can see in @fig-day-one — the silver band — and built outward. **The cell is the structure. The coloured panels hung on it aren't.** That's why the proportions look wrong to an eye trained on normal cars: you're looking at a passenger box with the mechanical parts pushed to the ends, rather than a long car with the middle removed.

It's also why the panels are a different colour. They aren't pretending to be structural, so they don't have to match.

<!-- KIM: why a Smart specifically? There were other small cars in 2010. What decided it? -->

## What everyone assumes it's for

People assume a car this size is for short trips in a crowded place. That's a fair assumption — it's what Mercedes designed it for, and it's what most of them do.

**And we owned one that did exactly that.**

```{r}
#| label: twofer
#| include: false

## TwoFer: from the leased-car gas log (a live Google Sheet, not yet in the corrected
## dataset -- see deferred.md). 7 fill-ups, 2014-03-22 to 2015-01-10.
twofer_miles <- 1209
twored_median_day <- round(median(twored_legs$odo_miles, na.rm = TRUE))
twofer_in_days <- round(twofer_miles / twored_median_day, 1)
```

**Two4Two** — we called it TwoFer — was leased in Honolulu in March 2014 and never left the island. It was **a stand-in**: something to drive at home until we could bring TwoRed across. Only short trips, and we kept no proper logs for it.

The lease ran thirty-six months and ended on **22 March 2017**. **TwoRed was handed to a shipping company in Seattle sixty-one days later.** The stand-in went back two months before the car it stood in for arrived.

What record there is — seven fill-ups between March 2014 and January 2015 — covers **`r twofer_miles` miles.** The lease allowed 22,500 over its whole term and the closing statement charged nothing for mileage at all, so whatever TwoFer did in three years, it wasn't much.

TwoRed's median driving day, on the mainland, was **`r twored_median_day` miles.**

**So TwoRed covered TwoFer's entire logged mileage in about four days of driving.** Same manufacturer, near enough the same car, and the difference isn't in the machine at all. It's in what we asked of it.



## Four cars, and not the sequence you'd guess

```{r}
#| label: fleet-dates
#| include: false

## every date from a document in data/<car>/ -- see fleet_ownership.csv
```

The Foreword introduced them. What matters here is the shape, and it isn't a relay.

**TwoRed, 23 July 2010.** Bought new in San Diego with four miles on the odometer. We still have it. **It has never been replaced** — that's the thing to hold on to, because the other three all arrived around it rather than after it.

**TwoFer, March 2014 to March 2017.** A three-year lease, in Honolulu, entirely inside TwoRed's life. A stand-in, not a successor.

**Bordeaux, 1 April 2019.** Leased first, then bought out at the end — Mercedes insisted on that procedure, presumably for reasons of their own. **It was ours from the first day of the lease and it still is.**

**Creamsicle, 15 September 2021.** Bought used — a 2016 car, five years old. Sold to family in October 2024.

**★ And there's a hole in the middle of that list.** TwoRed left the mainland in May 2017. Creamsicle wasn't bought until September 2021. **For four years and four months we had no car on the mainland at all**, and the long drives simply stopped.

<!-- KIM: what happened in those four years? The pandemic covers part of it but that's an
     assumption, not a finding. And why buy a mainland car again in 2021, from a dealer in
     Missouri, when the Lake San Marcos anchor was long gone? -->

So Creamsicle isn't TwoRed's replacement. **It's the resumption** — mainland driving picked up again after a four-year pause, starting from a different part of the country because the parking space that had organised everything was gone.

**That's the fleet argument, and it doesn't depend on any single car being good.** One car you like is taste. **Four, chosen and re-chosen across sixteen years — including one bought used, one leased twice over, and one still sitting in the garage — is a judgement.**

## Which brings us to the question

People who see the car say they like it. Then, almost always, they ask whether it's safe.

I have an answer. It involves Mercedes, and that steel cell, and a comparison to race cars, and I've given it many times standing next to the car with my hand on the silver part.

**Do they believe it? Maybe. Maybe not.**

That's the honest report, and it's why the next chapter doesn't stop at the engineering.
